stemMd:
> In 2024 the district court began holding small-claims hearings in the evening as well as during the day. Over the year, the share of hearings at which the defendant failed to appear fell from 30% to 18%. The court concludes that evening hearings reduced non-appearance by letting defendants attend without missing work.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the court's conclusion?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Daytime non-appearance stayed near 30%; nearly all of the fall came from evening hearings.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Staffing the evening hearings cost the court more in overtime pay than it had budgeted for.

options.label: C
options.textMd: In 2024 the court also began sending defendants text-message reminders of their hearing dates.

options.label: D
options.textMd: The number of small claims filed in the district rose slightly during 2024.

explanationMd:
The court credits the fall in non-appearance to one change, evening hearings. To strengthen that, you want evidence that ties the fall specifically to the evening hearings rather than to something that affected all hearings.

If the daytime non-appearance rate stayed close to 30% while almost all of the fall came from evening hearings, the improvement is located exactly where the new arrangement applies. Any general cause — a change in the kind of claims, a stricter attitude to defendants, a wider publicity campaign — would be expected to lower the daytime rate too. Its staying flat makes the evening hearings the most plausible cause.

**How to check.** Compare it with the choice about text-message reminders. Reminders would reach daytime and evening defendants alike and offer a rival explanation for the fall, which **weakens** the conclusion. The choice that strengthens it is the one that rules out such across-the-board causes by showing that daytime hearings did not improve.

distractorRationale.c: This weakens rather than strengthens the conclusion. Reminders introduced in the same year are an alternative cause that could explain the fall in non-appearance without any help from evening hearings.
distractorRationale.b: The cost of the evening hearings bears on whether they are worth running, not on whether they caused the fall in non-appearance. It leaves the court's causal conclusion exactly where it was.
distractorRationale.d: The conclusion concerns the share of hearings at which defendants failed to appear. A slight rise in the number of claims says nothing about that share or about why it fell.

accessibilityText: A strengthen question. The argument says that in 2024 the district court began holding small-claims hearings in the evening as well as during the day; over the year, the share of hearings at which the defendant failed to appear fell from 30 percent to 18 percent; the court concludes that evening hearings reduced non-appearance by letting defendants attend without missing work. The question asks which statement most strengthens the conclusion. The four answer options are: daytime non-appearance stayed near 30 percent, and nearly all of the fall came from evening hearings; staffing the evening hearings cost the court more in overtime pay than it had budgeted for; in 2024 the court also began sending defendants text-message reminders of their hearing dates; the number of small claims filed in the district rose slightly during 2024.

provenance.notes: Original strengthen item: the key localises the effect to the changed condition, ruling out across-the-board causes; one distractor is a rival cause that weakens, and two are irrelevant. Court and figures are invented.
